title: Runtime fallbacks & precision-mixing strategy for VPC/on-prem deployments
next_steps: Redwood to share precision-mixing runbook + canary checklist
Customer to provide 3 representative prompt sets and one failing prompt
Schedule in-cluster smoke benchmark in dev-VPC next Tues (Nov 11)
SE to provide model variant compatibility matrix and KV-cache sizing guidance
action_items: Priya:confirm KMS-HSM network policy & shared egress requirements:2025-11-10
header: Date: 2025-11-03 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~58m | Location: Zoom | Recording: yes
summary: In-depth technical review of quantization tradeoffs (INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ), runtime fallbacks, and best practices for VPC/on-prem deployments. Customer reported a 2-3% accuracy regression after INT8 conversion on their clinical summarization model. Discussed mitigation via precision mixing, KV cache warmup, batching SLOs, and canary/rollback tooling for private deployments.
topics: accuracy regressions post-quantize, mixed-precision fallbacks, runtime kernel selection, KV cache sizing/warmth, batching latency vs throughput, on-prem/VPC networking and KMS impacts
transcript:
00:00 Lena (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call... we have Marcus, Priya, Owen from Redwood. Hi Daniel, Aisha, Trevor, Marisol from Helios?
00:12 Daniel (Helios): Yep, thanks. We called because after the INT8 run last month we saw consistent drops on clinical case summaries, about two to three percent BLEU-ish equivalent, so hoping to understand whether that's AWQ/GPTQ artifacts or runtime mismatch.
00:30 Marcus (Redwood SE): Right, and to confirm — you ran our INT8 profile using the dedicated onprem package inside your dev VPC, is that correct?
00:38 Aisha (Helios): Correct. We used the Redwood private agent image, pinned the model version, and used the recommended AWQ pipeline from the docs. We also tried GPTQ from community scripts and saw similar but slightly different pattern.
00:50 Marcus: Okay. Two immediate axes: the quantization algorithm (GPTQ vs AWQ vs vendor int8) and the runtime execution path (kernel selection, fused-attn vs fallback). On private clusters kernel selection can be different if CUDA/cuDNN/ML libs don't match our verified profile.
01:10 Priya (Redwood SRE): Also worth calling out KV cache warmup — when you switch precisions the KV layout and caching heuristics can change, so early tokens will have different perf/accuracy.
01:22 Trevor (Security): Quick security note — we validated KMS integration but want to ensure the runtime fallback does not leak unencrypted cache to disk in edge cases.
01:30 Lena: Noted. We'll include an audit checklist.
02:05 Marcus: Can you walk us through the failing prompt pattern? Is it a certain length or entity type?
02:14 Aisha: Mostly longer clinical notes, multi-paragraph, and heavily enumerated medications. The output sometimes drops or mis-attributes dosage numbers — like 10 mg became 1o mg (o letter) in a handful of cases.
02:30 Owen (Redwood): That sounds like quantization rounding causing logit shifts on numeric tokens, usually a sign that the specific layer quantization or the outlier-aware quantization (O3 vs O2) wasn't capturing range.
02:45 Daniel: We also saw intermittent latency spikes when under load — the throughput fell and the latency SLO breached 250ms p95.
02:55 Marcus: Two separate but related issues: accuracy regressions and latency regressions. With batching and the KV cache, throughput will depend heavily on batch shaping and prefetch. For VPC/on-prem the network inter-node latency can amplify batching delays because some stages block on others.
03:20 Marisol (Ops): Our cluster is heterogeneous — a mix of A100-40GB and a couple of older A10s. Could that explain some kernel fallbacks?
03:29 Marcus: Definitely. Kernel selector picks optimized kernels per GPU capability. If a node doesn't have the expected compute capability or driver, the runtime falls back to a more generic path that may be slower and, in rare cases, suffer subtle FP fidelity differences when int8 emulation is used.
03:50 Marcus: Quick proposed troubleshooting plan: 1) reproduce the regression with a small eval set inside your dev-VPC; 2) capture kernel selection logs and per-layer quant stats; 3) run mixed-precision serving where the first N layers are FP16/FP32 and lower layers are INT8; 4) run a KV cache warmup profile and size adjustments.
04:10 Aisha: How invasive is mixed-precision? If we do first 4 layers FP16 and rest INT8, what's the perf hit?
04:20 Marcus: Typically you lose maybe 10-20% throughput compared to full INT8 but you often recover most of the accuracy. It depends on model shape. On A100 you may still see a net reduction in cost because INT8 tokens are cheaper, but latency under burst may increase due to kernel mismatches.
04:40 Daniel: Can we do an automated rollback if accuracy drops after a deploy?
04:48 Lena: Yes — Redwood supports automatic fallback to the last good variant at routing level. In private deployments we push a canary policy that monitors prompt-level metrics, and if the regression crosses threshold we route live traffic to the previous model and pin the suspect nodes.
05:05 Owen: Important note: in VPC we rely on the control-plane agent to flip the routing — so control-plane connectivity must be available. If you're fully air-gapped, the rollback is local — we provide a local-controller that can do the swap given sufficient privileges.
05:25 Trevor: That local-controller still needs to verify signatures from our KMS, does that require outbound egress?
05:32 Priya: If using an on-prem HSM, the local-controller will call the HSM via your LAN; no outbound internet egress needed. We'll provide the stub for your security team to review.
05:52 Speaker 3: (inaudible) mention of operator-level flags for kernel pinning...
06:15 Marcus: One gotcha: AWQ sometimes optimizes per-channel scales differently than GPTQ and can produce different quantization grids. So even if both claim INT8, the perceptual error distribution differs. That explains why you saw similar but non-identical failures.
06:40 Aisha: For our failing prompt, GPTQ seemed slightly better on named entities, AWQ slightly better on long-range coherence. Strange.
06:50 Marcus: Yup. Also, the runtime's KV cache normalization can interact with quantization — if KV cache is stored as reduced precision (e.g., INT8 backed) we sometimes apply per-key scaling that changes effective attention weights.
07:10 Daniel: Is there an easy test to know if KV cache is the culprit?
07:16 Marcus: Yes: serve with KV cache disabled for a few tokens (or cold start every request) and compare outputs. If accuracy improves, it's the cache interaction. Also run profiling with cache-hit ratio and per-token logits diffs.
07:40 Aisha: We tried cold starts in QA and saw little difference, but our QA prompts were shorter. We'll reproduce with the longer clinical prompts.
07:52 Marcus: Also collect per-layer outlier counts — spikes indicate channels that need wider quant bins; we can then do per-channel scaling or switch those layers to FP16.
08:10 Marisol: On the latency side, our autoscaler sometimes spins up older A10 nodes under load which are slower. Any recommendations?
08:20 Priya: Best practice: pin instance types in the Dedicated cluster or configure homogeneous pools for latency-sensitive routes. Mixed pools are okay for best-effort traffic but not for low-p95 SLOs.
08:34 Marcus: Another trick is runtime-aware routing: route low-latency requests to FP16 pools and batch/throughput requests to INT8 pools. That ties into canarying and routing policies.
08:48 Daniel: Can we get a sample config for that?
08:52 Lena: We'll send the sample routing policy and an example canary that looks at per-prompt BLEU/QA metrics.
09:04 Aisha: What about FP8? We experimented with FP8 on a small set but saw instability. Is FP8 mature for production?
09:12 Marcus: FP8 can give good density but requires library/kernel support. On A100 Ampere, FP8 kernels are emerging but driver mismatch leads to nondeterministic results. For now FP8 is experimental in private deployments unless you match the exact stack versions we support.
09:34 Marcus: If you need FP8 density, our recommendation is: do a controlled bench with pinned drivers, enable FP8 only on homogeneous pool, and have a fallback to FP16/INT8.
09:46 Daniel: Any recommended thresholds for rollback? 
09:50 Owen: We typically set a canary threshold of 1% absolute drop on key metrics or a 3-sigma deviation on response token distributions for sensitive applications. For clinical text we recommend a lower tolerance — 0.5% absolute or double-check via manual review.
10:10 Marisol: For long-term, is there tooling to automate mixed-precision placement per-layer?
10:16 Marcus: Yes — Redwood Optimize includes a layerwise sensitivity scan that proposes which layers to keep FP16. We'll run that on your model and return a candidate mixing table. That usually reduces manual back-and-forth.
10:34 Aisha: How long does the sensitivity scan take?
10:38 Marcus: For a 30B-ish model, a full scan can take a few hours on dedicated infra; a faster heuristic scan is possible in 30-90 minutes. We'll propose both.
10:50 Daniel: On canary metrics — how do we compute prompt-level accuracy automatically? Our clinical metrics are custom.
10:58 Lena: You can push custom eval callbacks — Redwood supports webhooks for per-prompt labels or batch offline evals. For private, we can configure that to run inside your VPC and keep data in your storage.
11:20 Trevor: Security question — if we send example prompts to Redwood for troubleshooting, what guarantees on PII?
11:26 Lena: We recommend anonymizing; but if necessary we can consume under a Data Processing Addendum and store only in your encrypted buckets. We'll provide the security pack and DPA text.
11:40 Aisha: Back to the regression — we'd like a triage plan with clear isolation steps.
11:45 Marcus: Right, stepwise triage we propose: environment parity check (drivers, libs), reproduce with minimal eval, isolate quant algorithm (run FP16 baseline, AWQ, GPTQ, vendor-int8), KV cache toggle, layerwise mixed-precision, and finally canary deploy. We'll script most of this.
12:10 Marisol: Can the runtime generate a per-request manifest to trace which kernel + quantizer were used?
12:18 Owen: Yes, the runtime emits a manifest per request — kernel id, per-layer scale tables, KV-cache version. In private deployments we can increase verbosity. Be careful with logs retention and PII.
12:36 Aisha: That manifest would be invaluable. Please include an example.
12:40 Marcus: We'll attach a sample manifest in the follow-up.
12:50 Daniel: On mixed pools, can the routing layer do token-level switching or only request-level?
12:56 Marcus: Currently request-level only. Token-level switching is theoretically possible but not productionized because of KV consistency issues. Token-level would require identical KV representations across pools.
13:14 Trevor: Are there any known issues with quantized models and FIPS / HSM environments?
13:20 Priya: No direct conflicts; KMS/HSM handles keys. The only concern is if you offload parts of preprocessing to a secure enclave the inference stack must be compatible. We'll run a compliance checklist.
13:40 Speaker 2 (Customer): (muffled) question about model version pinning...
14:00 Marcus: About model pinning — always pin both model artifact and quantization profile. We saw cases where model weights auto-updated in artifact registry and the quant profile was stale leading to mismatches.
14:20 Aisha: That might explain some of our intermittent diffs. We'll audit registry permissions.
14:30 Marcus: Next, batching — if your tail-latency is key, tune max batch size low and use priority lanes for low-latency routing. For throughput-bound tasks, maximize batch and use prefix caching aggressively.
14:50 Daniel: What's the impact of prefix caching on accuracy for long clinical notes?
14:58 Marcus: If prefix caching reuses past KV with different precision, tokens at the border can be slightly off. Warm cache with representative prefixes to reduce this. Also, per-prefix quant stabilization helps.
15:10 Aisha: Any special consideration for tokenization? We saw occasional splits that made numbers ambiguous under quantization.
15:18 Marcus: Yes — tokenization differences can amplify quant errors. Make sure the tokenizer runtime is identical across all nodes and pinned. Tokenizer mismatch is a surprisingly common root cause.
15:40 Daniel: Ok, to summarize can we list immediate experiments?
15:45 Lena: Sure: 1) Run FP16 baseline on dev-VPC for the failing prompt; 2) Run AWQ and GPTQ with per-layer manifests; 3) Run mixed-precision candidate (first 4 layers FP16) and measure; 4) Run KV cache disabled vs warmed; 5) Provide kernel selection logs and manifest.
16:10 Aisha: We'll prioritize 1-3 this week and upload results.
16:18 Marcus: We'll prepare the runbook and a canary configuration for you and include rollback playbook and manifest examples.
16:25 Marisol: Also please include recommended autoscaler pool config for homogeneous latency pools.
16:30 Priya: We'll add the KMS/HSM network checklist and local-controller docs.
16:36 Trevor: Security will review the DPA and run the local-controller through pen test if needed.
16:42 Lena: Great. Any final questions?
16:48 Daniel: One last — are there any quick wins to reduce accuracy regressions without touching quant?
16:54 Marcus: Yes: better prompt engineering (normalizing numeric formats), forcing canonical tokenization for meds, and targeted post-processing checks for critical fields. These often fix many of the numeric misreads.
17:10 Aisha: Awesome. Thanks everyone.
17:15 Lena: Thanks — we'll follow up with the runbook, manifests, and sample configs.
17:22 Meeting end.
